title: Rook against pawn
summary: The cut-off, counting tempi, the shoulder and the defence that promotes to a knight.
part.cutting.title: Cut off or get behind
part.cutting.summary: The rook cuts off the black king or gets behind the pawn while the king comes.
part.counting.title: Count and shoulder
part.counting.summary: One tempo decides everything: count the moves and shoulder the black king away.

part.saavedraEnd.summary: When the pawn beats the rook, the three rules and the ending in the practical challenge.
step.t_cut: The pawn is racing to promote and your king is far away. How can the rook gain the time your king needs to arrive?
step.t_cut.hint1: Look for a rank where the rook stands between the black king and the pawn's path.
step.intro: Rook against pawn looks easy: a rook is worth far more than a pawn. But the pawn walks on its own, and the rook needs its king to win. So this ending is a race: if your king arrives in time, the rook wins; if it arrives late, the pawn queens or costs the rook, and it is a draw. Before you move, ask three questions. Can I cut the black king off with the rook? How many moves does my king need to reach the pawn? And is the black king in front of the pawn or behind it? Here the black king is still far from d1, and the rook can separate it from the pawn.
step.cut: Cut the black king off. The rook on a rank between the king and the pawn's path leaves the pawn alone, and a lone pawn is food for the rook. Then bring your king.
step.cut.hint: 1.Ra5: the fifth rank is now off limits for the black king. Then 2.Kg6.
step.cut.done: The black king cannot cross the fifth rank. If the pawn runs, the rook catches it; if the black king walks around, your king is already there. Cutting off is the first tool: it costs one move and gains several.
step.behindIdea: When you cannot cut the king off, put the rook behind the pawn. It stops the pawn from moving without an escort: at every step, the black king has to stand next to it to defend it. And while the black king babysits the pawn, your king, which is far away, gains the tempi it was missing.
step.behind: Rook behind the pawn, then the king on its way.
step.behind.hint: 1.Rc8, behind the pawn. Then the king comes: 2.Ka7.
step.behind.done: Rook behind the pawn and king on its way. The black king has become the pawn's nanny, and your king will arrive before the pawn queens.
step.race: Now there is no cut and no shortcut: you count. The pawn needs three moves to reach f1. Your king has to arrive in time to help the rook win the pawn. The shortest way is diagonal, towards the squares in front of the pawn. Lose one move and the sums no longer add up.
step.count: Count and run. Your king has exactly the moves it needs, not one more.
step.count.hint: 1.Kc6, 2.Kd5 and 3.Kd4: always diagonally, towards the pawn.
step.count.done: Just in time. The white king stands next to the squares the pawn has to cross, the rook goes to the f-file, and the pawn falls. Notice that any other first move would already have drawn.
step.late: The same position with your king one square further away. Now the sums do not add up: whichever way it goes, your king arrives one move later than needed, and the black king escorts the pawn to the end. It is a draw. In this ending a single tempo decides everything. That is why you count before you play.
step.bodycheck: When both kings race to the same place, push with your shoulder. The black king wants to reach d3 and d2, next to the pawn. Your king can step into its way: it takes the squares the black king needs, and the black king is left outside, far from the pawn. That is the shoulder: your king pushes the other one away without touching it.
step.shoulder: Put your king in the black king's way and stay there.
step.shoulder.hint: 1.Kd5, attacking the pawn. After 1...c3, 2.Kc4, which takes d3 from the black king. After 2...c2, 3.Kc3.
step.shoulder.done: The black king never got near the pawn. Your king stood between them, and the rook finishes the job.
step.block: The shoulder works for both sides. Here it is the black king that blocks the way: on e5 it rules out d6 and e6, and your king cannot go through there. Do not force it. Walk around by the c-file, in front of the pawn, and use the rook to hold the pawn from behind.
step.around: Go around the black king, hold the pawn with the rook and arrive in front.
step.around.hint: 1.Kc6, going around the black king. Then 2.Rd1 behind the pawn, 3.Kc5 and 4.Kc4.
step.around.done: You went around the black king's shoulder and arrived in front of the pawn. With the rook behind and the king in front, the pawn has nowhere to go.
step.tempo: Sometimes the black king stands on the perfect square, in front of the pawn, and your king cannot arrive in time. That is when the tempo-gaining check comes in. The rook checks and forces the black king to pick a side. Whichever it picks, it leaves the front of the pawn, and that one move is exactly what your king needed.
step.check: Give the tempo-gaining check and bring the rook back behind the pawn.
step.check.hint: 1.Re8+. After 1...Kf3, the rook goes back behind the pawn: 2.Rd8.
step.check.done: The check moved the black king away from the front of the pawn. Now it needs a move to come back, and in that move your king walks around and arrives.
step.t_knight: The white king has arrived and the rook threatens mate. It looks lost for Black. Does Black have any resource that saves the game?
step.t_knight.hint1: Promoting to a queen loses. Think of a promotion that comes with check.
step.knight: Now the other side. Black has lost the count: the white king has arrived and the rook threatens mate on a1. Promoting to a queen loses at once: 2.Ra1 is mate. But there is 1...e1=N+, checking the white king. The knight sticks to its own king, the rook cannot separate them, and it is a draw. Whoever defends with the pawn has to know this resource; whoever has the rook has to avoid falling for it.
step.rush: This is how you fall into the trap. White had a winning position and rushed the king to e3. The black king went to e1, and 2.Rh8 seemed to win, threatening mate on h1. But then came 2...d1=N+, with check, and the knight saved everything. The hurry took the king to e3, exactly a square where the newborn knight gives check.
step.trap: The same position, before the mistake. Win without giving the knight a chance.
step.trap.hint: Do not move the king yet. 1.Rd8, behind the pawn. After the black king goes to c2, 2.Ke2 and 3.Rxd2.
step.trap.done: The rook attacked the pawn from behind and the white king arrived via e2, where no knight check gains anything. First the rook, then the king.
step.t_saavedra: Now the pawn is yours, against the rook. It is two steps from promoting, but the rook keeps harassing. How does the pawn win?
step.t_saavedra.hint1: Watch out for stalemate after the promotion. Not every promotion has to be a queen.
step.saavedra: A curiosity to finish. As a rule, pawn against rook is the pawn fighting for a draw. But there is the Saavedra position, from 1895, in which the pawn wins. After 1.c7 and a series of checks, Black sets up a stalemate: if the pawn becomes a queen, the rook offers itself and no move is left. Saavedra found the answer: promote to a rook. No stalemate, and a mating threat. The knight promotion you saw today is a cousin of that idea: sometimes the smaller piece is worth more.
step.recap: Three rules. One: first of all, cut the king off with the rook, or put the rook behind the pawn. Two: count the tempi; your king walks diagonally, and if the black king blocks the way, use your shoulder or go around in front of the pawn. Three: beware of the knight; do not take your king to a square where the promotion gives check.
step.finish: Now it's you, in the practical challenge. Cut off the black king or put the rook behind the pawn, count the tempi and beware of the knight.
ex.e11: Black to move and win. This time the rook is yours, and the white pawn is still on g2. The white king wants to get close to it. Don't let it.
ex.e11.hint: A rook can cut along a file too. Which file separates the white king from the pawn?
ex.e11.solution: 1...Rf7+. The check drives the white king off the f-file, and the rook stays there as a wall. The toughest defence is to go to the e-file, and from there it can't get back to the pawn; on the g-file, next to the pawn, it loses even faster. The pawn is left alone, your king walks down calmly and the rook wins the pawn. Any other move lets the white king reach the pawn in time, and it's a draw. Position from the study "Rook versus Pawn" by Kyrylo27 on Lichess.
ex.e12: White to move and win. A rook pawn, and your king is on the other side of the board. Find the missing tempo.
ex.e12.hint: Before putting the rook behind the pawn, force the black king out of the way.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Rg6+. The black king must leave the g-file: if it goes to the h-file, it stands in front of its own pawn and slows it down; if it goes to f3, the rook gets behind the pawn with 2.Rh6 (2.Rf6+ also wins). With the pawn held, your king arrives via c5, d4 and e3. 1.Rh6 right away is one tempo late: the black king escorts the pawn and it's a draw. Position from the study "Rook against Pawns" by Anki_Thief_of_Crowns on Lichess.
ex.e13: Black to move and draw. The pawn is pinned on the second rank and the white king protects the rook. It looks hopeless. Find the saving move.
ex.e13.hint: Sometimes having no legal move at all is the best defence.
ex.e13.solution: 1...Kh1!, into the corner. If White takes the pawn with 2.Rxg2, the black king has no square and it's stalemate; if not, White can't make progress. 1...Kh3 loses the pawn to 2.Rxg2, and 1...Kg1 loses after 2.Rxg2+, with the rook protected by the king. It's the typical knight-pawn draw: the king in the corner, next to the pawn. A test from the study "Principles of Rook vs Pawn Endgame" by Ezryn on Lichess.
ex.e14: White to move and win. There's a free rook check. Does it help?
ex.e14.hint: Where would the check send the black king? Think about who reaches the squares in front of the pawn first.
ex.e14.solution: 1.Kd6! Your king heads for the squares in front of the pawn; after 1...Ke4, the rook gets behind the pawn with 2.Rg7 (2.Re7+ also wins), and the white king comes via d5 and d4. The check 1.Rd5+ looks natural, but it sends the black king to f4, exactly where it wanted to go: in front of the pawn, with your king behind. Then it's a draw. Not every check gains time; the one that gains time is the check that moves the king out of the way. Position from the study "Rook versus Pawn" by Kyrylo27 on Lichess; there the main line is 1.Rd5+, and the tablebase says only 1.Kd6 wins.
ex.e15: White to move and win. Now the pawn is yours, and the black rook is checking. Where does the king go?
ex.e15.hint: Two traps: the pin on the seventh rank and the check on the b-file after promotion. The king has to walk towards the rook.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Kc5! After 1...Ra5+, 2.Kc4; the checks go on with 2...Ra4+ 3.Kc3 Ra3+ 4.Kb2, and then they run out: the pawn promotes. The king walks down a staircase towards the rook. 1.Kb5? throws away the win to 1...Ra1: if 2.b8=Q, 2...Rb1+ and the queen falls. 1.Kc7? allows 1...Ra7, pinning the pawn, and 1.Kd5? allows 1...Rb6, winning the pawn. This is Zukertort's analysis of the game Fenton–Potter, 1875, the position the Saavedra study grew out of. As given on Wikipedia.
ex.e16: Black to move and draw. Kamsky–Bacrot, Sofia, 2006. The white king is coming for the pawn and the rook is ready. Defend to the end, one move at a time.
ex.e16.hint: First, use your king to block the white king's path. At the end, when a queen can't be born, remember there are other pieces.
ex.e16.solution: 69...Kf3!, the shoulder: the black king takes the squares the white king would walk through. After 70.Rh8, 70...e3; after 71.Rh3+, 71...Kf2; after 72.Kf4, 72...e2; after 73.Rh2+, 73...Kf1; and after 74.Kf3, 74...e1=N+!, with check. Each of these is the only move that holds. Promoting to a queen at the end loses: 75.Rh1 is mate. Rook against knight, with the knight next to its king, is a draw. In the game Bacrot found the knight, but went wrong later and lost.
ex.e17: White to move and draw. The pawn will become a queen and nothing can stop it. Even so, there is a draw. Where does the rook need to be?
ex.e17.hint: Your king protects more than one square on the sixth rank. A protected rook that checks forever doesn't need to win anything.
ex.e17.solution: 1.Ra6!! After 1...c1=Q, 2.Rb6+; after 2...Ka3, 3.Ra6+, and so on, along the a- and b-files. The rook is always protected by the king on b7, and the black king can't get away: if it steps onto the c-file, Rc6+ puts the rook in front of the queen, which can only be saved by trading itself for the rook. Other moves lose: the queen is born and the black king escapes the checks. Position from the study "Rook versus Pawn" by Kyrylo27 on Lichess.
key.cut: The cut-off: the rook sits on a rank between the black king and the pawn and keeps it from helping while the white king makes its way over.
key.shoulder: The shoulder: the white king walks right next to the black king and pushes it away from the squares beside the pawn.
key.check: A check at the right moment: the rook drives the black king back, and the white king gains the tempo it was missing.
key.knight: The defender's resource: promoting to a knight, with check, saves the draw. Promoting to a queen would lose.
key.saavedra: Saavedra, 1895: here the pawn beats the rook. Promoting to a queen would stalemate the black king; promoting to a rook wins.
history: Rook against pawn looks easy: a rook is worth far more than a pawn. But if the rook's king is far away and the pawn well advanced, there is often not enough time, and a single move separates a win from a draw. The most famous case is an exception: in 1895 a Glasgow newspaper published a rook-against-pawn position as a draw, and a Spanish priest living in the city, Fernando Saavedra, showed that the pawn actually won, by promoting to a rook instead of a queen so as not to stalemate the enemy king. Ever since, the Saavedra position has been one of the best-known studies in chess. In everyday games the rule is simpler: with the king close, the rook wins; with the king far away, you have to count the moves.
practice: Now the practical challenge: rook against pawn, and your king is far away. Count the tempi, walk diagonally and give the knight no chance. The goal is to win.
